title: The Role of the Crowd in Countering Misinformation: A Case Study of the COVID-19 Infodemic
screen_reason: Observational Twitter study of COVID-19 misinformation and counter-misinformation. Although the paper develops a text classifier as one of its contributions, its aim is to characterise the misinformation ecosystem, and its sample-description table (Table V) reports the composition of a keyword-collected corpus of 155,468 English COVID-19 tweets: 33,237 classified as misinformation. That is a share of items classified as misinformation with a stated denominator, i.e. a CONTENT estimate, so the paper is eligible under the rule that a study whose aim is something else is still included when a descriptive share is reported. Flagged borderline because the classifier-development framing sits close to the 'detection work' exclusion.

estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-19 keyword-collected English tweets classified as misinformation tweets
estimates.value_raw: 33,237 misinformation tweets of 155,468 total tweets (Table V; by topic: 5G 24,606/97,283 = 25.3%, fake cures 8,631/58,185 = 14.8%)
estimates.denominator: 155,468 English-language, non-retweet tweets from 105,772 users, collected 21 Jan - 20 May 2020 via COVID-19 keywords (COVID-19, covid, corona virus, coronavirus) combined with misconception-entity keywords (5G, drinking water, ginger, garlic, salt) from the Twitter Streaming and Search APIs
estimates.definition: A tweet was labelled a misinformation tweet if it supported an IFCN-verified false COVID-19 claim about fake cures or 5G, or otherwise contained falsehoods, inaccuracies, rumours, decontextualised truths or misleading leaps of logic; assignment was by a logistic-regression classifier on BERT embeddings with a strict >0.5 score rule
estimates.misinfo_def: "we consider misinformation tweets to include falsehoods, inaccuracies, rumors, decontextualized truths, or misleading leaps of logic, all regardless of the intention of the spreader"
estimates.source_quote: Total number of tweets 97,283 58,185 155,468 Number of Misinformation Tweets 24,606 8,631 33,237
estimates.page_loc: Table V, TWITTER DATA STATISTICS (columns: 5G, Fake Cures, Total); the same counts appear in the Section V closing sentence and in the Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors hand-labelled 4,800 tweets (2,400 per topic) as misinformation / counter-misinformation / irrelevant, with a 300-tweet double-coded overlap giving Cohen's kappa = 0.782; those labels trained three one-vs-all logistic-regression classifiers on BERT embeddings, applied with a >0.5 score rule. Reported test F1 for misinformation detection: 0.775 +/- 0.02 (5G) and 0.694 +/- 0.03 (fake cures); the authors summarise overall F1 as 0.7-0.8. Ground truth for the underlying false claims came from 6,840 IFCN CoronaVirusFacts fact-checks reduced to 57 fake-cure and 32 5G claims.
estimates.moderator_quote: Similar to [37], we utilized a keyword-based method to collect COVID-19-related tweets. ... COVID-19 keywords: this set includes widely-used terms associated with COVID-19, such as: COVID-19, covid, corona virus, coronavirus [37]. Misconception entity keywords: 5G, drinking water, ginger, garlic and salt.
estimates.notes: The corpus is deliberately enriched for misinformation: the keyword list combines generic COVID terms with the entities named in the false claims (5G, garlic, ginger, drinking water, salt), so this share is the composition of a two-topic misconception-keyword corpus, not a prevalence in COVID discourse at large. Hence denom_scope=topical with denom_selection=curated, and confidence medium. Labels are classifier-assigned (F1 0.69-0.82), so the share carries classifier error in both directions. Value is an exact part/whole from verbatim Table V counts. INTERNAL ARITHMETIC NOTE for the adjudicator: Table V's 'Total' for citizen counter-misinformation tweets should be 34,413 (26,229 + 8,184), not the 33,413 printed in the table and abstract; every other column and row sums exactly, and 33,237 + 441 + 34,413 + 87,377 = 155,468. This typo does not affect the extracted numerator or denominator. borderline=true because the paper also presents itself as classifier/dataset work, which is close to the detection-work exclusion. QUOTE NOTE: source_quote is the Table V row pair carrying both denominator and numerator. The prose statement of the same counts is split by interleaved figure text in this rendering; its contiguous fragment reads 'that contains 33,237 misinformation tweets, 33,413 counter-'.

missed_or_uncertain: Deliberately not extracted: (a) Per-topic splits from Table V (5G 24,606/97,283 = 25.3%; fake cures 8,631/58,185 = 14.8%). They are verbatim and could each be a row, but both are the same country x platform x construct x topic (covid19) cell, so I kept the pooled headline figure to avoid triple-counting the same corpus; the exact per-topic counts are recorded in value_raw so an adjudicator can split if the review prefers topic-level rows. (b) '5 of the Top 20 most-frequent sources are listed as low-credibility' (Figure 1, misinformation tweets) and '7 of the Top 20 most frequent sources are known high credibility' (counter-misinformation tweets). These are annotations of a rank-truncated top-20 domain figure computed inside an already-misinformation-only subsample, with no exposure or item denominator behind the 20; a 5/20 count is not a usable prevalence, so I recorded it here rather than as a within_misinfo_content row. (c) '96% of refuting tweets are generated by concerned citizens', '67% of citizen responses do not contain any evidence', 'only 33% of citizen response tweets have URLs, out of which only 4% point to fact-checking websites', and '204 of [300 sampled URLs] provided reliable evidence, of which 96 contained links to high-credibility sources' - all describe who counters misinformation and with what evidence, not the prevalence of misinformation. (d) 'most of the tweets received 0 retweets (71% - 80%), while only few tweets were retweeted more than 100 times (0.2% - 0.6%)' - engagement distributions, not misinformation shares, and not a concentration statement of the top-X%-to-Y%-of-activity form required by R1. (e) Verified-account shares (misinformation 1%, professional fact-checkers 22%/8%, concerned citizens 7%/4%) and follower means - account attributes. (f) 'only around 10% of the tweets have links' - link prevalence. (g) IFCN's 6,840 fact-checked false statements and the Avaaz claim that top-10 health-misinformation websites got four times the views of reputable organisations - the first is an all-false set with no denominator, the second is a figure cited from elsewhere (excluded per R8).

rob.design: Retrospective observational analysis of an ~8-million-tweet keyword crawl (Twitter Streaming API 1% sample augmented by Search API) reduced to 155,468 English, non-retweet tweets from 105,772 users, 21 Jan - 20 May 2020, on two topics (5G conspiracy, fake cures) whose false claims came from 6,840 IFCN fact-checks (57 fake-cure + 32 5G claims). Labels: 4,800 tweets hand-coded by two authors over several iterations with reconciliation meetings, 300-tweet overlap kappa = 0.782; logistic regression on BERT embeddings, five-fold cross-validation, misinformation-detection F1 0.694-0.775, applied with a >0.5 decision rule. No response rate applies. Limitations for prevalence use: the sampling frame is misconception-keyword enriched, non-English tweets and retweets are dropped, and all labels below the 4,800 hand-coded seed are machine-assigned.
rob.item6_quote: Misinformation Tweets: Since in this research we are interested in identifying a broader set of COVID-19 misinformation tweets, we consider misinformation tweets to include falsehoods, inaccuracies, rumors, decontextualized truths, or misleading leaps of logic, all regardless of the intention of the spreader.
rob.item10_quote: Applying the classifier as described above returns a dataset that contains 33,237 misinformation tweets, 33,413 counter-misinformation tweets, and 441 professional fact checking tweets (see Table V).
